title: Kura–Araxes and the Bronze Age Caucasus
subtitle: 3,500–1,200 BC · Shengavit, the Trialeti Kurgans and the Wagons of Lchashen

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No kings survive, only cultures — the Kura–Araxes world, the kurgan princes of Trialeti, the fortress builders of Sevan, and the polities that Hittite and Assyrian texts name

entries.label: The Kura–Araxes horizon
entries.hint: From about 3500 BC a distinctive culture of mudbrick villages, red-black burnished pottery and portable hearths spread over the valleys of the Kura and Araxes, from the Caspian lowlands and the Lesser Caucasus to the Armenian plateau. Some sites, like Kültepe in Nakhchivan, run from the late Chalcolithic into it. It had no evident capitals or kings, and is known entirely from its settlements and burials.
entries.note: Antonio Sagona, The Archaeology of the Caucasus (2018); Philip Kohl, The Making of Bronze Age Eurasia (2007); Adam T. Smith, The Political Machine (2015).

entries.label: Nakhchivan — Ovçular Tepesi and Kültepe
entries.hint: In the Araxes valley around Nakhchivan, Ovçular Tepesi, with its large Chalcolithic settlement of the fifth and fourth millennium, and the Kültepe mounds, with their long Kura–Araxes sequence, show the continuity from the farming villages of the Neolithic to the Bronze Age horizon. The area was also a place of exchange between the Kura and the Mesopotamian world.
entries.note: V. Aliyev, Nakhchivan archaeological studies; B. Lyonnet et al., Ovçular Tepesi reports (2017–); Sagona 2018.

entries.label: Shengavit — a walled town on the Hrazdan
entries.hint: On a rock spur above the Hrazdan in Yerevan, Shengavit grew from a village into a settlement of about six hectares, with round and rectilinear mudbrick houses on stone footings, a massive wall with towers, and a sanctuary with hearths and cult objects. Excavated by Sardarian in 1936–1958 and again from 2009 by an Armenian–American team, it is the best-known Kura–Araxes site in Armenia.
entries.note: Sardarian, Shengavit reports (1936–1958); M. Rothman and H. Simonyan, Shengavit excavations (2009–2012).

entries.label: The Bedeni and Martkopi cultures
entries.hint: After the Kura–Araxes settlements declined in Kartli, the plateau of Bedeni and the neighbouring highlands held herders who buried their dead under large kurgans with wagons, horse bones, and gold and silver ornament. The Martkopi culture, a little earlier, has the first of the big kurgans. Their burials mark a society with strong differences in rank.
entries.note: A. Kakhiani, 'Bedeni Culture' studies; Sagona 2018; Kohl 2007.

entries.label: The Trialeti–Vanadzor culture
entries.hint: The kurgans of Trialeti on the Tsalka plateau, excavated from 1936 under Boris Kuftin, held a wooden wagon, weapons, and vessels of gold and silver, and have given their name to a culture of the Middle Bronze Age found in south Georgia, north Armenia (Vanadzor, Lori) and Javakheti. Its princely burials contrast with the many modest graves of the same period.
entries.note: B. Kuftin, Trialeti excavation reports (1941–47); A. Kushnareva, The Southern Caucasus in Prehistory (1997).

entries.label: Lchashen–Metsamor
entries.loc: Lake Sevan and the Ararat plain
entries.hint: In the later second millennium, the settlements of Lake Sevan, the Ararat plain and Syunik built stone-walled hillforts and cemeteries with rich bronze weapons. Metsamor, in the Ararat plain, was a major centre with metalworking and a walled citadel, and Lchashen on Sevan had a fortress and the cemetery that held wooden wagons. This culture is the background of the later highland states.
entries.note: A. Kushnareva 1997; Sagona 2018; Metsamor excavation reports (Khanzadian, Areshian).

entries.label: The Colchian culture
entries.hint: On the humid Black Sea plain of western Georgia a Bronze Age culture of the Colchis lowlands and the Rioni valley made distinctive socketed axes of bronze, some of which reached the north Caucasus and Anatolia, and lived in timber houses. It is the root of the Iron Age Colchian culture of the first millennium.
entries.note: O. Lordkipanidze, Archäologie in Georgien (1991); Sagona 2018.

entries.label: Hayasa-Azzi in the Hittite texts
entries.hint: Hittite cuneiform names a land of Hayasa-Azzi on the upper Euphrates and the highlands beyond it, with kings, cities and fighting forces; in the reign of Suppiluliuma I the Hittites made a treaty with its ruler Hukkana. The land has been identified by some scholars with the early Armenians because of the similarity of 'Hayasa' to 'Hay', the Armenian self-name, a link which others reject.
entries.note: Hittite treaty with Hukkana of Hayasa (CTH 42); Billie Jean Collins and others on Hittite texts; Kohl 2007.

entries.label: Uruatri and the Nairi lands
entries.hint: Shalmaneser I of Assyria (1274–1245) reports in a royal inscription a campaign against the land of Uruatri, a group of eight lands in the mountains to the north, which he claims to have subdued. It is the earliest known mention of the name later given as Urartu. The rest of the Assyrian record calls these regions Nairi, 'the land of rivers'.
entries.note: Royal inscriptions of Shalmaneser I (RIMA 1); Paul Zimansky, Ancient Ararat (1998).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Walls at Shengavit, cyclopean fortresses and the Hittite and Assyrian wars on the highlands

entries.label: The first walls
entries.hint: Kura–Araxes settlements, among them Shengavit, were protected by stone walls and towers, and the weapon types of the later period, daggers, spearheads and mace-heads, show that war was a regular occurrence. The stone circuits might also have served as protection for livestock and as a statement of ownership.
entries.note: Rothman and Simonyan, Shengavit reports; Sagona 2018.

entries.label: The cyclopean fortresses
entries.hint: Late Bronze Age builders of the highlands put up hillforts of huge unmortared stone blocks, in the so-called cyclopean style, at Lchashen, Metsamor, Tsakahovit and Sisian and in dozens of other places, with walls several metres thick and towers. Their number points to endemic rivalry between local chiefdoms.
entries.note: Kushnareva 1997; Sagona 2018.

entries.label: The Hittite wars against Hayasa and Azzi
entries.hint: The annals of Suppiluliuma I and Mursili II tell of campaigns against the kings of Hayasa and Azzi, whose border raids troubled the Hittite northeast, and of the treaty that bound Hukkana. They show a highland polity that could confront a great power.
entries.note: Annals of Suppiluliuma I and of Mursili II (Hittite royal annals); Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (1998).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Village layouts, kurgans that rank the dead, and the first treaty text to name a highland ruler

entries.label: The village and the household
entries.hint: A Kura–Araxes settlement was a cluster of single-family houses, round or square, with a central hearth, a bench and storage pits, in some sites joined into a larger complex. Differences in house size or wealth are small, suggesting that the households were the basic economic unit, with only weak inequality.
entries.note: Sagona 2018; Smith, The Political Machine (2015).

entries.label: The kurgan elite
entries.hint: The Bedeni and Trialeti kurgans, mounds up to 100 metres across and several metres high, hold single burials with wagons, weapons, drinking vessels and precious metal; around them are modest graves. The scale and wealth of these tombs are the clearest evidence in the region for the appearance of a hereditary elite.
entries.note: Kuftin 1941–47; Kushnareva 1997; Kohl 2007.

entries.label: The treaty with Hukkana
entries.hint: A tablet from Hattusa records the terms imposed by a Hittite king on Hukkana of Hayasa: he must give up Hittite captives, not give shelter to fugitives, supply troops, and he was bound to the king's family by marriage to the king's sister. It is the oldest written document that treats the highland ruler as a party to a treaty.
entries.note: CTH 42, Treaty between Suppiluliuma I and Hukkana; G. Beckman, Hittite Diplomatic Texts (1999).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The hearth and the sanctuary, the oxen and wagons of the kurgan, and the stone fish of the springs

entries.label: The Shengavit sanctuary
entries.hint: A group of rooms near the centre of Shengavit contained hearths with clay supports, animal horns, figurines and a built platform. The excavators interpreted it as a ritual area dedicated to the hearth and probably to ancestors. Portable andirons with horns or animal heads are common across the Kura–Araxes world and likely served a hearth cult.
entries.note: Rothman and Simonyan, Shengavit reports; Sagona 2018.

entries.label: The wagon and the ox in the kurgan
entries.hint: In the big kurgans a wooden four-wheeled wagon, sometimes with the bones of the oxen that drew it, was placed in or beside the grave of a single person together with vessels and arms, a custom of the steppe zone to the north. They suggest a belief in a journey after death and the display of wealth in funerals.
entries.note: Kuftin 1941–47; Kushnareva 1997; Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007).

entries.label: The vishap stones
entries.hint: High in the Geghama and Aragats mountains, near springs and meadows, stand huge stone stelae shaped like fish or bulls' heads, up to five metres long, called 'vishapakar' or dragon stones in Armenian. They were probably put up in the second millennium by herders in a cult of water and fertility; their dating is uncertain.
entries.note: H. Martirosyan, Armenia in the Bronze and Early Iron Ages; Armenian Academy of Sciences surveys of vishapakars; A. T. Smith, R. Badalyan and P. Avetisyan, The Archaeology and Geography of Ancient Transcaucasian Societies (2009).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The red-black burnished ware, the silver and gold cups of Trialeti and the wagons of Lchashen

entries.label: Red-black burnished ware
entries.hint: The Kura–Araxes potters made handmade vessels with a black interior and red exterior, burnished to a shine, decorated with ridges and incised spirals and bands. The ware, found from the Caucasus to Syria, is the cultural fingerprint of the horizon.
entries.note: Sagona 2018; Kohl 2007.

entries.label: The silver cup of Trialeti
entries.hint: A silver goblet from the great kurgan of Trialeti, in the Georgian National Museum, is engraved with a frieze of figures in animal skins and masks in a ritual procession before a deity. A gold goblet inlaid with precious stones comes from another princely kurgan there. Their iconography has Near Eastern parallels.
entries.note: Kuftin 1941–47; Kushnareva 1997; Georgian National Museum collection.

entries.label: The wagons and boats of Lchashen
entries.hint: In the 1950s the lowering of Lake Sevan exposed Late Bronze Age kurgans at Lchashen that held complete wooden wagons and models of chariots, preserved under water, and small bronze and wooden models of boats, animals and people. They are the best preserved Bronze Age vehicles in the Near East and are shown in the History Museum of Armenia.
entries.note: Kushnareva 1997; History Museum of Armenia, Lchashen collection.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The question of the first Armenians, the Kartvelian languages and a stone circle read as an observatory

entries.label: The question of the first Armenians
entries.hint: When Indo-European speakers reached the Armenian plateau, and from where, is unresolved. Linguists place Armenian as a distinct branch of Indo-European, and scholars have proposed arrival from the steppe in the third or second millennium, or from the west in the late second, associated with Phrygian movements; others locate speakers of its ancestor in the region from much earlier. The identification of Hayasa with the Armenians is also disputed.
entries.note: Robert Drews, The Coming of the Greeks (1988); James Clackson, Indo-European Linguistics (2007); Kohl 2007; Armen Petrosyan, The Problem of Armenian Origins (2002).

entries.label: The Kartvelian languages
entries.hint: Georgian, Mingrelian, Laz and Svan, the Kartvelian family, are unrelated to any other known language family despite attempts to link them to others, and their ancestor is generally placed in the southern Caucasus by the third or second millennium. Its date of break-up is debated.
entries.note: A. Harris (ed.), The Indigenous Languages of the Caucasus, vol. 1: The Kartvelian Languages (1991); G. Klimov, Etymological Dictionary of the Kartvelian Languages (1998).

entries.label: Karahunj and the observatory claim
entries.hint: At Karahunj (Zorats Karer) above the Vorotan gorge near Sisian, about 200 standing stones, some with drilled holes, form a circle with lines radiating from it, around Bronze and Early Iron Age graves. The radio-physicist Paris Herouni argued the holes sighted on sun and stars and dated the site to about 7500 BC, calling it an 'Armenian Stonehenge'. Archaeologists date the site to the Bronze and Iron Ages as a necropolis and reject the astronomical claim.
entries.note: P. Herouni, Armenians and Old Armenia (2004); Armenian excavation reports of the graves; critical reviews by archaeologists.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Arsenical bronze, mobile herding and the copper of the Lesser Caucasus

entries.label: Arsenical bronze and the copper of the Lesser Caucasus
entries.hint: The ores of the Lesser Caucasus, at Kedabek in Azerbaijan, in Syunik and in Kvemo Kartli, made the region one of the main producers of metal in West Asia. Smelters made arsenical copper and later tin bronze in workshops such as Metsamor, with ingots and finished weapons traded far outside.
entries.note: Kohl 2007; Sagona 2018; E. Chernykh, Ancient Metallurgy in the USSR (1992).

entries.label: Mobile herding
entries.hint: By the third millennium many households practised seasonal movement, taking sheep, goats and cattle to high summer pastures such as Ughtasar and Aragats and back to winter villages in the valleys, as shown by animal bones, camp sites and rock art. The system remained the basis of highland farming in later periods.
entries.note: Sagona 2018; Smith 2015; Kohl 2007.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The wheel, bronze casting, cyclopean masonry and the portable hearth

entries.label: The wheel and the wagon
entries.hint: Wheeled wagons appear in the Caucasus by the fourth millennium, in the Maykop kurgans of the north and in the south in the tombs of Bedeni and Trialeti, with solid disc wheels, and by the Late Bronze Age spoked wheels and light chariots are found at Lchashen. The region is one of those claimed as an early centre of the vehicle.
entries.note: Anthony 2007; Kuftin 1941–47; Kushnareva 1997.

entries.label: Bronze casting and cyclopean masonry
entries.hint: Smiths of the Late Bronze Age cast socketed axes, spearheads, swords and decorated belts in stone and clay moulds, and builders raised fortress walls of massive roughly dressed stones without mortar. Metsamor has furnaces, moulds and a walled citadel.
entries.note: Kushnareva 1997; Sagona 2018.
keywords: Smiths of the Late Bronze Age

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Kura–Araxes spread to Anatolia, Iran and the Levant, the Maykop north and the Near Eastern courts

entries.label: Maykop and the north
entries.hint: North of the main range, the Maykop culture of the Kuban buried a chief in a great kurgan with gold, silver and copper vessels and beads of carnelian and turquoise, and contacts with the south introduced metal and techniques into the Kura–Araxes region. Maykop lies in the north Caucasus, outside this folio's zone, and appears here as a neighbour.
entries.note: Kohl 2007; Rezepkin, Maikop culture studies; Sagona 2018.

entries.label: The Kura–Araxes diaspora
entries.hint: Kura–Araxes pottery and houses appear far outside the home region: at Karaz near Erzurum, at Arslantepe, at Yanik Tepe in Iranian Azerbaijan and, as Khirbet Kerak ware, at Beth Yerah and other sites in the Levant. Whether this represents migration of people, of herders or only of a style is a long-standing dispute.
entries.note: Burney and Lang, The Peoples of the Hills (1971); Rothman (ed.), Uruk Mesopotamia and Its Neighbors (2001); Kohl 2007; Sagona 2018.

entries.label: The goods of the Near Eastern courts
entries.hint: The princely burials of Trialeti and of the later Lchashen contain beads of carnelian and lapis lazuli, cylinder seals and ornaments, with parallels in Mitanni and Hurrian contexts in northern Mesopotamia. They show that the highland chiefs took part in the prestige-goods exchange of the Near Eastern world.
entries.note: Kushnareva 1997; Kohl 2007.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The dry centuries around 2200 BC and the end of the Late Bronze Age world

entries.label: The dry centuries around 2200 BC
entries.hint: A pronounced aridity phase, the 4.2 ka event, is documented in cave and lake records from Mesopotamia to the Caucasus, and is linked by some scholars to the abandonment of many Kura–Araxes settlements and to the move of populations to higher ground and pastoral life. The decline began in some regions earlier, and the causal role of climate remains debated.
entries.note: H. Weiss et al., Science 261 (1993); Sagona 2018; Kohl 2007.

entries.label: The end of the Late Bronze Age order
entries.hint: In the decades around 1200 BC the Hittite state collapsed and the palace economies of Syria and the Aegean fell, and the Mitanni and Hittite powers that had treated with the highland rulers vanished. The centuries which followed saw the rise of Assyria and, in the highlands, of new states that wrote in their own inscriptions.
entries.note: Eric Cline, 1177 BC: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014); Bryce 1998.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Households and figurines, and the kurgan dead

entries.label: Figurines and the household
entries.hint: Small clay figures of humans and animals, among them many female figures, come from the houses and sanctuary of Shengavit and other Kura–Araxes sites. They are commonly connected with household ritual, fertility and the hearth, though their meaning is conjectural. Women are known in this world from their figurines and burials, not from any text.
entries.note: Rothman and Simonyan, Shengavit reports; Sagona 2018.
